<reason>PRO (Side B) built the cleaner path to victory. Its core frame—cascades are a threshold crossed by accumulation, so every permanent fragment counts and tests are the only wholly optional source—was never dislodged. CON's strongest line, that the treaty cannot "prevent" cascades because wartime intercepts stay legal, was neutralized by PRO's symmetry point: CON's own preferred disposal/traffic rules share the hole and are compatible with the treaty, not competitors, so the hole cannot rank the instruments. CON then conceded under A2 that none of its instruments stop a deliberate smash either. Most damaging was CON's A1 answer to the benefit question: a "credential" that "does not have to outweigh a 2007-style cloud," which PRO correctly read as conceding the harm is real while offering almost nothing against it. CON's definitional attack was answered plausibly (orbiting target vs suborbital warhead; the fragments are the evidence), and CON's India 2019 example cut against it. PRO's clipped turns were a minor execution cost but lost only trailing sentences. CON was disciplined and rhetorically sharp ("changing the photo, not the physics") but stayed on a demanding standard PRO showed nothing meets.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B3.2/B4.3 pressure—the wartime hole applies equally to CON's disposal alternative—forced CON's admission in A4.3 that none of its instruments stop a deliberate smash, collapsing CON's "fatal hole" into a bar that disqualifies every instrument and therefore cannot decide the motion; paired with CON's A4.1 "does not have to outweigh" concession, it left PRO's cost-benefit comparison essentially unopposed.</best_rebuttal>
